passages.where: Going through the towns teaching and healing, Jesus sees the crowds and is moved with compassion, because they are harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. The site's plain note says he looked at crowds and felt compassion, not irritation, and then told his disciples to pray for workers. What he felt moved him to act.

Seeing his brother Benjamin for the first time in more than twenty years, Joseph is moved to tears and hurries to a private room to weep, then washes his face and comes back. The site's note says the scene shows the pressure building inside the disguise. Deep feeling held in for a long time does not disappear; it finds a room.

Hounded by enemies who twist his words, David asks God to put his tears in a bottle and says they are written in God's book. The site's plain note says the verse is for anyone who has cried where no one saw: God saw, and not one tear was wasted or forgotten. Tears that embarrass us are kept by God.

Among Paul's short commands about sincere love is this pair: rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. The site's plain note on 2 Corinthians 4 quotes it against handing a verse to someone in fresh grief. Feeling another person's sorrow is not a weakness to outgrow; it is what love is asked to do.

Singing songs to a heavy heart, the proverb says, is like taking off a coat on a cold day or pouring vinegar on a wound. The site's note sets it among the Hezekiah collection's comparisons on words well spoken and restraint. Scripture expects some hearts to feel the wrong word keenly, and asks everyone else to notice.

The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy. The site's note says many sayings in Proverbs are observations rather than commands, and this one names the heart's hidden bitterness and joy. It is one reason feeling a great deal can be lonely: much of it cannot be fully shared.

After listing beatings, dangers and hunger, Paul says he faces daily the pressure of concern for all the churches: who is weak, and he is not weak; who is led into sin, and he does not burn with grief. The site's plain note says his proof that he served Christ was not his success but what he had suffered and how much he cared. The apostle counted feeling for others among his marks of service.

Jeremiah wishes his head were a spring of water and his eyes a fountain of tears, so that he could weep day and night for his people. The site's note on the chapter says he longs for endless tears for them and then wishes he could escape them. A prophet who felt this much also wanted, at times, to get away from it, and Scripture keeps both.

Peter tells all believers to be like-minded and sympathetic, to love as brothers, and to be tenderhearted and humble. The site's note on the chapter says he calls the whole church to unity and compassion. Tenderness is a command for everyone, not a flaw in a few.

The letter says Christians do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with their weaknesses, but one tempted in every way as they are, yet without sin. The site's plain note says the weaknesses meant are human frailties, not sins, and that he knows tiredness, hunger, grief, betrayal, fear and pain from the inside. The one who hears our prayers is not numb to what we feel.

misread.taken: Guard your heart is given to people who feel things deeply as a reason to toughen up: feel less, keep what moves you to yourself, and treat strong feeling itself as the danger.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says that in Hebrew thought the heart was not mainly the seat of emotion, as it is in English, but the center of the inner person, where a person thinks, decides, remembers and desires. Guarding it means guarding one's whole inner orientation, the source from which choices, words and actions flow, and the father goes on to speak of the mouth, the eyes and the feet. It is a call to watch over the direction of a life, not a command to feel less.

whole: Some people feel everything more than those around them. A harsh word stays with them for days; a story about strangers keeps them awake; they can tell a room has gone tense before anyone speaks, and they are worn out by noise and crowds that others hardly notice. Many have been told since childhood that they are too sensitive, too much, that they should toughen up. Some have tried, and found that hardening themselves made them colder without making them stronger. Others feel deeply and do not know what to do with it, so it comes out as worry, tears at the wrong moment, or withdrawal.

Scripture does not share the suspicion of deep feeling. Jesus looked at the crowds and was moved with compassion; Joseph, seeing his brother after twenty years, hurried out of the room to weep; Jeremiah wished his eyes were a fountain of tears for his people; Paul said that when another was weak he was weak, and when another was led into sin he burned with grief. The letter to the Hebrews says Christ is able to sympathize with our weaknesses. Proverbs observes that the heart knows its own bitterness and that no stranger shares in its joy, which is part of why feeling much can be lonely. The trouble is rarely the depth of feeling itself. It is what a person has come to believe about it: that it is shameful, or that it must always be obeyed, or that no one could understand it.

So the Bible's wisdom is neither to harden the heart nor to be ruled by it. Guard it, Proverbs says, meaning the whole inner self from which choices and words flow, not the feelings alone. Weep with those who weep, Paul says, which is a gift many sensitive people already have; and Proverbs warns against singing cheerful songs to a heavy heart, a mistake they rarely make. It helps to tell God about each tear, as David did when he asked God to keep his tears in a bottle, and to tell a trusted friend rather than carry it alone. It helps to step away from noise when it is too much, as Jesus withdrew from the crowds to pray. And when strong feeling turns into worry that will not settle, a doctor or a counsellor can help, and seeking that help is not a failure of faith.

The hope Scripture gives is that tender hearts are in good company. Peter tells the whole church to be tenderhearted, and the high priest who stands for us is not unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. God keeps account of every tear, and not one is wasted or forgotten. The same heart that feels the world's pain keenly is often the one most able to carry someone else's, and in Christ it was never meant to carry all of it alone.
sit: Where have you been told you feel too much, and what would it mean to bring that feeling to God instead of hiding it from him?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says verse 8 is an invitation to pour out your heart before God: not tidy prayers, everything. Pray it with whatever you are feeling today.
